Volume 09 · Chapter 12

Investment policy and portfolio integration

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v09-c11

By the endDefend a mandate and portfolio using economic objectives and robust evidence.
Capability objective. Defend an investment mandate and a feasible portfolio using dated liabilities, an implementable benchmark, explicit risk and cash limits, reproducible evidence, and accountable reporting. A portfolio decision is complete only when its cash commitments, implementation and authority to act also reconcile.

Prerequisites. Execution, trading costs and market microstructure; the covariance and optimization tools in Chapter 2 and Chapter 3; performance evaluation; and the liability, horizon and illiquidity reasoning in Chapter 9 and Chapter 10. This chapter explains its finite optimization and funding rules locally.

1. Begin with what the investor must be able to do

A committee receives a portfolio with an attractive expected return and a low reported volatility. Six months later a grant is due, but the assets cannot be redeemed. Alternatively, the manager holds extra cash and reports lower total risk, while moving farther from the committee's chosen benchmark. Neither problem is visible in an expected-return ranking alone. The mandate must connect the investor's purpose to assets, dated payments, acceptable failures and the people permitted to respond.

An investment policy statement (IPS) records that connection before outcomes arrive. Separate three kinds of statements. A policy judgment chooses objectives, priorities, limits and authority. A mathematical implication follows from specified inputs and contracts. An evidence claim concerns whether those inputs describe the world and how reliably they were estimated. An exact optimizer proves the second; it does not prove the first or third. The CFA Institute's May 2010 IPS discussion supports a customized document tying investor objectives to governance, constraints, risk monitoring and reporting. Its examples and thresholds are not adopted here.

Our original case is the Larch Research Reserve, a fictional grant fund. Its current decision covers one year, followed by a fresh committee review. It does not promise perpetual spending or preservation of real purchasing power. Every currency amount is in kCU, thousands of fictional currency units. Rates are decimal simple returns unless otherwise stated. There are no taxes, exchange-rate changes, undisclosed fees or current legal requirements. Actual institutions would need evidence and applicable contractual/legal review beyond this teaching case.

The fund has 1,000 kCU immediately before the date-0 trade. It inherits equity exposure 300, bond exposure 400 and cash 300. Its mission requires a planning grant of 150 at date 1, one half-year later, and 50 at date 2, one year later. Grants are distributions for the mission, not investment fees. At date 2 the committee wants a remaining reserve of at least 650 in specified design stresses. It also requires 20 of cash immediately after the date-1 grant. These limits express this board's preferences and contingency planning; they are not universal safe levels.

2. Make dates, costs and the opportunity set explicit

The available equity and bond sleeves are funded one-year mandates. Invest x and y kCU at date 0. All their proceeds arrive at date 2; there is no interim redemption, sale or pledge. Their supplied terminal returns include all exit dealing costs. This is a deliberately finite contract, not a claim that ordinary traded equities and bonds must be held for a year. Larch selects x in {0,10,…,500} and y in {0,10,…,600}. Positions are long only. There are no derivatives or additional committed capital calls in this menu.

Cash earns 1% in each of two equal half-year periods, a full-year factor g² = 1.0201 with g = 1.01. Entry costs are 1% of equity turnover and 0.5% of bond turnover, deducted from cash at date 0. The self-financing budget is

K(x,y) = 0.01|x−300| + 0.005|y−400|,
c = 1000−x−y−K(x,y),   x+y+c+K = 1000.

Costs apply to amounts traded from inherited holdings, not to the total selected holdings. Posttrade investment wealth is 1000−K. The weights x/(1000−K), y/(1000−K), c/(1000−K) sum to one. For the risk budget below, however, the board uses original pretrade wealth 1000 as the fixed denominator. Mixing these denominators changes the meaning of a percentage limit.

A fictional emergency facility makes at most 25 kCU available at date 1 only. There is no commitment fee. Each unit drawn costs 1.08 at date 2: an 8% cost for this borrowing half-year, not an annual rate. Borrowed cash may count toward the 20 buffer. The facility cannot fund initial positions; ordinary portfolio feasibility must satisfy the listed design cases with no borrowing or external contribution. Its purpose is a separate contingency bridge. These exact availability and repayment assumptions are indispensable to the model.

Let L1 and L2 denote a scenario's grants, D its date-1 loan draw and X an external contribution at date 1. Cash first earns g, then X and D arrive, then L1 is paid. At date 2 the remaining cash earns g and the mandates distribute; L2 and the loan are then paid. With scenario returns rE and rB,

C1 = gc+X+D−L1,
A2 = x(1+rE)+y(1+rB),
R2 = A2+gC1−L2−1.08D.

R2 is the final cash reserve. A negative hypothetical C1 is not an authorized overdraft. If resources do not pay the grant, report a dated funding failure and leave the later executed reserve unavailable until a repair is specified. Similarly, a loan adds D to cash and creates a repayment obligation; it cannot be counted as investment profit. Contributions are external financing and must remain visible as equal contributor outlays.

3. A filled policy, with a feasible benchmark

The following is Larch's completed instructional IPS for this decision. It is intentionally brief enough that a manager, treasurer and reviewer can use the same rules. The attachments are the exact input file, model, ranked alternatives and dated stress ledger, rather than unstated intentions.

Larch policy adopted at date 0; all limits are original case choices
Policy itemFilled decision rule
Purpose and horizonPay the one-year research grants and preserve a reserve for the next annual allocation decision. Nominal kCU accounting; no perpetual or inflation-adjusted guarantee.
Assets and obligationsInitial wealth 1,000; inherited equity/bond/cash 300/400/300. Planning grants 150 at date 1 and 50 at date 2. The treasurer owns the dated grant register.
Permitted implementationTwo one-year funded mandates, cash and the contingent line specified above. Ten-kCU lots, equity cap 500 and bond cap 600, nonnegative cash after entry fees. No other borrowing or interim asset pledge.
Strategic comparisonImplement 400 equity and 400 bonds from the inherited portfolio; pay fee 1 and retain cash 199. Hold these mandates through date 2 and apply the same grant dates. Freeze this benchmark before execution.
Decision criterionRank feasible portfolios by expected final reserve minus 4/(2×1000) times reserve variance, using the disclosed synthetic planning moments. Retain alternatives and sensitivity results.
Risk authorizationOne-year total standard deviation at most 100 kCU; active standard deviation at most 6 kCU against the implemented policy portfolio, both based on the supplied covariance. These are 10% and 0.6% of initial wealth.
Liquidity and stress floorAfter the largest date-1 planning/design grant, hold cash at least 20 without the line. In each listed design stress, reserve after all date-2 obligations is at least 650. Additional stresses must be reported even if they fail.
Contingent fundingThe treasurer may prepare a draw up to 25 for a documented date-1 need, with both-date cash proof and committee approval. A draw must repay 1.08 per unit at date 2. New contributions require a separate explicit commitment.
Delegation and conflictsThe committee approves policy, assumptions, grants and exceptions. The investment officer recommends the portfolio and submits orders within the mandate. The treasurer reconciles cash and obligations. A reviewer independent of order entry checks positions, fees and risk; manager compensation and related-party interests are disclosed before appointment.
Execution and exceptionsBefore the date-0 dealing window closes, recompute the filled portfolio, including unfilled orders. Any mandate breach triggers immediate committee escalation. No manager may repair a breach by changing the benchmark or labeling an unauthorized loan as cash.
Monitoring and rebalancingReview cash commitments monthly and before each grant; recalculate scenarios when grant terms or relevant assumptions change. No interim trading of locked mandates is authorized. At date 2, all mandates mature to cash and the committee authorizes a new policy decision; the previous year's target is not an automatic instruction to buy.
Report and audit trailPreserve approved inputs, orders/fills, fee/cash records, benchmark, deviations, stress gaps and action owners. Report actual, intended and benchmark outcomes at identical dates. Amendments have dated reasons and apply prospectively; exceptions remain in the historical record.

Calling the policy “40/40/20” is shorthand for a pre-cost target. The actual comparator is 400/400/199 after fee 1. An invented cash position of 200 would overstate its terminal reserve by 1.0201. An ex-ante benchmark must also be feasible for this investor's dates and costs; Sharpe's benchmark discussion motivates that comparison, not a claim that this board's allocation is uniquely correct. The original 300/400 holding is an inherited starting point, not automatically compliant with the new active-risk mandate.

4. Derive the risk budget and the decision criterion

The planning means are μ = (0.10,0.06) and the one-year simple-return covariance is

Σ = [[0.04,0.006],[0.006,0.01]],   det(Σ) = 0.000364 > 0.

These moments have a coherent original finite witness. Let Z equal ±1 with probability ½. Independently let U equal ±0.13 with probability 7/26 each, or zero with probability 6/13. Define rE = 0.10+0.20Z and rB = 0.06+0.03Z+U. E[U] = 0, Var(U) = (7/13)(0.13²) = 0.0091, so Var(rB) = 0.0009+0.0091 = 0.01 and Cov(rE,rB) = 0.20×0.03 = 0.006. The six joint probabilities sum to one and every return exceeds −1. This witnesses internal consistency; it is neither empirical estimation nor a claim that actual outcomes must have this finite support.

For h = (x,y)ᵀ and the fixed planning grants, random reserve differs from hᵀr only by deterministic terms. Therefore its mean M and variance v are

M = 1.10x+1.06y+1.0201c−1.01(150)−50,
v = hᵀΣh = 0.04x²+0.012xy+0.01y².

Let hb = (400,400)ᵀ and a = h−hb. Under common return scenarios and matched grants, active reserve equals aᵀr plus deterministic position/cash/cost terms, so its variance is vA = aᵀΣa. Entry-cost differences affect the active mean and wealth, not this variance. The annual limits are v ≤ 10,000 and vA ≤ 36, in kCU squared. There is no square-root annualization from a monthly sample here. Were grants random and correlated with returns, reserve variance would also contain liability variance and covariance; our moment model fixes planning grants, while separate stress scenarios vary them explicitly.

Capital allocation and risk allocation differ. For σ(h) = √(hᵀΣh) > 0, differentiating gives ∂σ/∂hi = (Σh)i/σ. Define the volatility contribution RCi = hi(Σh)i/σ. Summing yields ΣRCi = hᵀΣh/σ = σ. The numerators hi(Σh)i similarly sum to variance. They split each covariance term symmetrically. Negative contributions can occur for a hedge; they do not imply negative standalone variance. At the zero portfolio σ = 0, these derivative contributions are undefined, although total variance is zero. They are accounting sensitivities conditional on Σ, not causes of realized returns.

The committee chooses the mean-variance score

J(h) = M(h) − [γ/(2W)]v(h),   γ = 4,   W = 1000.

M is in kCU; v/W is also in kCU, so the dimensions reconcile. Larger γ penalizes risk more. The earlier mean-variance reference provides context; our exact decision proof depends on the finite feasible set, not on a claim that this score fully describes preferences. Equal moments can conceal different tails, and the hard cash and stress limits protect features a variance score alone omits.

Ordinary feasibility requires the position bounds and grid, c ≥ 0, both variance limits, gc ≥ 180+20, and R2 ≥ 650 in each design stress below, with D = X = 0. The largest date-1 bill includes both planning and design cases. Costs are included before testing liquidity. There are only 51×61 = 3,111 candidate pairs. Evaluate every pair, discard all violations, rank the remainder by exact J, and use lower variance, lower fee, then lower x and y to resolve a tie. Proof of the certificate: every permitted pair appears once in this finite enumeration; every constraint is evaluated; any feasible alternative is therefore among the ranked records and cannot exceed the first score. This proves a grid optimum. It makes no claim of a continuous, unrestricted, all-state or true-preference optimum.

Worked example 1 — Cash, risk and benchmark authorization

Consider x = 370 and y = 430. Equity turnover is 70 and bond turnover 30, giving K = 0.70+0.15 = 0.85. Cash is 199.15, and 370+430+199.15+0.85 = 1000. At date 1 cash becomes 201.1415. Paying the largest design grant 180 leaves 21.1415, exceeding the required buffer by 1.1415.

Σh = (17.38,6.52)ᵀ. Variance contributions are 6430.6 and 2803.6, totaling 9234.2. Standard deviation is approximately 96.094745 kCU, or 9.6094745% of original wealth. Dividing those contributions by the standard deviation gives 66.919372 and 29.175373 kCU. The equity sleeve carries about 69.64% of total variance despite receiving only 37% of initial wealth.

Active positions are (−30,+30); Σa = (−1.02,0.12). Active variance is 30.6+3.6 = 34.2, with standard deviation 5.848077 kCU, below 6. Using standalone volatility alone would omit both the sign of the active positions and the covariance term.

The benchmark buys 100 equity, leaves bonds unchanged, pays 1 and holds 199 cash. Its variance is 9920; cash after the grant of 180 is 20.99. Its active variance against itself is zero. Its worst listed terminal reserve will be 653.1999, so the comparator is feasible. By contrast, inherited (300,400) has active positions (−100,0), hence active variance 400. A transition is required even though its total variance, 6640, is lower. “Lower volatility” alone does not determine mandate compliance.

Worked example 2 — Choose among genuinely feasible alternatives

The exact enumeration finds 28 feasible pairs. For 370/430, the mean reserve is 407+455.8+203.152915−201.5 = 864.452915. Its penalty is 4×9234.2/2000 = 18.4684, giving J = 845.984515. The first three ranked alternatives and the policy benchmark are:

Feasible portfolio comparison; amounts kCU, variances kCU squared
x / yCashMvvAJ
370 / 430199.15864.4529159234.234.2845.984515
370 / 420209.20864.1049209104.832.8845.895320
380 / 420199.10864.8019109455.215.2845.891510
400 / 400 benchmark199.00865.4999009920.00845.659900

The winner has 1.046985 less expected reserve than the benchmark, but its risk penalty is 1.3716 lower; its score is therefore 0.324615 higher. Maximizing expected return and maximizing this chosen score are different decisions. The runner-up gap is only 0.089195 kCU. Exact arithmetic eliminates rounding ambiguity; it does not make a small modeled difference economically certain.

Holding all constraints and moments fixed, γ = 2 selects 400/400, while γ = 6 selects 370/400, whose mean is 863.408930, variance 8852 and score 836.852930. These are preference changes. Subtracting two percentage points from every equity witness return instead changes a forecast mean, preserving covariance; with γ = 4, 370/430 remains selected but mean falls to 857.052915 and score to 838.584515. The exact feasible ranking can be reproduced; no single optimizer output determines which preference or forecast the board should approve.

5. Connect stress losses to dated shortfalls

A stress scenario specifies jointly what happens to assets and required cash. It is not a marginal asset shock pasted onto unchanged liabilities without discussion. Larch's two design scenarios have no assigned probabilities: equity fall uses rE = −30%, rB = +5%, grants 150/50; inflation/funding uses −15%, −12%, grants 180/60. They are separate from the moment witness. Calling the second “inflation” identifies the assumed joint adverse mechanism; the numbers are not an estimated inflation transmission law.

For selected positions, the first reserve is 370(0.70)+430(1.05)+1.0201(199.15)−1.01(150)−50 = 712.152915. The second is 370(0.85)+430(0.88)+203.152915−181.8−60 = 654.252915. Both clear 650. The benchmark produces 701.4999 and 653.1999. The two paths are feasible; neither portfolio is guaranteed to clear the floor in an unlisted event.

The selected inflation path falls 210.2 below the planning mean reserve. Of that, 92.5 is the equity change 370(0.10−(−0.15)), 77.4 is the bond change 430(0.06−(−0.12)), and 40.3 is the extra grant burden 1.01(180−150)+(60−50). This is a cash explanation of a conditional difference. Subtracting final reserve from initial wealth would combine mission distributions with investment outcomes; calling the whole amount an investment loss would be misleading.

For any selected c, a date-1 bill preserving buffer B without outside contributions must satisfy L1 ≤ gc+D−B. Thus the selected holding supports 181.1415 with no line and 206.1415 with the full 25 line. Permitting cash to fall to zero instead allows payment of 226.1415; that is a different condition and breaches the buffer. A terminal wealth estimate cannot pay a bill before the mandates distribute.

Worked example 3 — Reverse stress and a repair that closes both dates

Now test an event outside the design set: equity −25%, bonds −8%, grants 240 at date 1 and 60 at date 2. Before the first payment cash is 201.1415; even drawing 25 provides only 226.1415. The payment shortfall is 13.8585. To pay the bill and retain the 20 buffer, the funding gap is 33.8585. These are different failures. With no additional funding, there is no executed terminal reserve to report; compounding a negative cash balance would invent an unapproved loan.

Suppose a contributor actually provides 33.8585 at date 1 while the line is fully drawn. The bill is now paid and cash 20 remains. At date 2, equity pays 277.5, bonds 395.6 and cash 20.2. The grant is 60 and loan repayment is 27. The reserve is 606.3, still 43.7 below 650. Repairing today's liquidity alone does not repair the end-date policy.

For any permitted D, write A = 277.5+395.6 = 673.1. Requiring both C1 ≥ 20 and R2 ≥ 650 gives the exact minimum contribution:

X(D) = max{0, 240+20−201.1415−D,
[650−673.1−203.152915+1.01(240)+60+(1.08−1.01)D]/1.01}.

With D = 25 this is 15,579,417/202,000 ≈ 77.125826733. Cash after date 1 becomes 6390/101 ≈ 63.267327; its date-2 proceeds 63.9 plus the mandates 673.1 pay 60+27 and leave exactly 650. With D = 0, the contribution is smaller: 15,229,417/202,000 ≈ 75.393153465. Cash after date 1 is 3690/101 ≈ 36.534653; its date-2 proceeds are 36.9, so 673.1+36.9−60 = 650. Both schedules exceed the interim buffer.

The no-line case minimizes external contribution here. The terminal bound is already binding at D = 0 and increases by (0.07/1.01)D; the decreasing cash bound stays below it. Borrowing 25 would therefore add 175/101 ≈ 1.732673267 to required external funding. More generally X(D) is the maximum of zero, a decreasing cash bound and a nondecreasing terminal bound. Its minimum on [0,25] occurs at an endpoint, their crossing, or a flat zero region. The lab checks these candidates exactly. Cheap immediate liquidity is not free terminal wealth.

This is a conditional funding requirement, not evidence that a contributor exists. The committee must obtain a commitment, renegotiate grants or revisit authorized policy; the manager cannot silently manufacture financing. A contribution improves the fund's reserve and imposes an equal external cash outlay. A performance report must disclose it and use the same contribution date in any matched investor comparison.

6. Govern implementation and revise policy without rewriting history

A recommendation should state an action, the assumptions making it defensible, the alternatives and the condition that would change it. Larch's committee can authorize the 370/430 target with its budget and finite-scenario limits while recognizing its thin advantage over nearby alternatives. The investment officer does not have authority to change γ, the strategic comparison or the grant schedule to make a trade pass. Separating approval, order entry and independent reconciliation makes the decision reviewable without pretending that a spreadsheet is a governing body.

Monitoring is not always rebalancing. At date 0, actual filled positions can be checked before the dealing window closes. After entry, the stipulated mandates cannot be redeemed or pledged; a rule saying “rebalance immediately after every adverse return” would contradict the asset contract. At date 1, only cash, the approved contingent facility and committed contributions are available. At date 2 all mandate proceeds become cash, so the board can evaluate a fresh allocation with new liabilities, costs and information. If it wants interim discretion, it must choose a different opportunity set prospectively and pay its costs.

Review triggers include changed grant dates, loss of an assumed funding source, contradictory or stale valuation data, an execution deviation, a revised covariance/forecast supported by evidence, and an unlisted stress exposing an unacceptable gap. The response begins with reconciling what changed. A favorable return after an unauthorized position does not erase the breach; an adverse return on an authorized position does not by itself prove bad judgment. Document the exception, the owner of the remedy, a deadline and whether the remaining policy is still feasible.

Evidence governance applies to inputs as well as trades. A real estimate needs its source, vintage, return/currency definitions, fees, missing observations, selection rules, estimation method and uncertainty. Do not tune expected returns until a favored portfolio wins, select only surviving managers, or treat an in-sample factor intercept as a priced opportunity. A forecast challenge should be recorded alongside the original forecast and tested with information available at the decision time. The synthetic witness here avoids fabricated observations but cannot substitute for that empirical work.

Worked example 4 — A complete exception and outcome report

The officer submits the intended 370/430 allocation, but one 10-kCU equity purchase is unfilled. Actual holdings are 360/430. Fee is 0.60+0.15 = 0.75 and cash is 209.25. Total variance falls to 8890.6; active positions (−40,+30) produce variance 58.6, above 36. The higher cash balance and lower absolute risk do not cure the benchmark-relative breach. This is a report of a failure requiring escalation, not an approved alternative.

If the remaining trade can actually be completed before the date-0 window closes under the stated fee schedule, buying the additional 10 and paying 0.10 restores the target. An assumed later fill is not a remedy under a no-interim-trading contract. For the outcome audit, suppose the breach was escalated but the partial portfolio remained invested, and returns were equity +12%, bonds +1%, with ordinary grants 150/50. Preserve the exception even if a committee temporarily permits holding the filled position.

The actual-minus-benchmark reserve gap is −4.043975. Insert the intended decision as an intermediate comparator:

Ractual−Rbenchmark
= (Rintended−Rbenchmark)+(Ractual−Rintended)
= −3.146985−0.896990 = −4.043975.

The first term is the conditional policy-selection effect; the second is the implementation effect. The missed purchase would return 10×1.12 = 11.2. Actual cash retains 10 plus the saved 0.10 fee and grows to 10.1×1.0201 = 10.30301, so the implementation gap is −0.89699. The unfilled target remains part of the comparison, as in Chapter 11's shortfall logic. This is not a claim that a fee-free purchase was available.

The report's action field reads: “Investment officer: preserve the unfilled order and explain nonexecution; independent reviewer: confirm fees, holdings and the 58.6 active-variance breach; committee: record the exception decision and revise execution arrangements before the next allocation.” The treasurer confirms both grants were paid and no loan existed. The archive retains all three portfolios; the benchmark is unchanged.

These are exact matched-date wealth differences, not estimates of skill. No interim mandate values were supplied, so the report does not invent a time-weighted return. Reliable values immediately around the grant boundary would be needed for that calculation. The previously inspected flow-boundary methodology explains why external flows and fees need explicit perimeters; no standards compliance is asserted. One realized conditional outcome cannot establish performance persistence or validate the forecast distribution.

7. Reproduce the committee file

Download the exact original inputs, standard-library analysis, complete reference output, contract and instructions and provenance/hash manifest. Keep the files together and run:

python3 v09-c12-analysis.py --input v09-c12-inputs.json
python3 v09-c12-analysis.py --input v09-c12-inputs.json --output answer.json

The first command prints the full report; the second writes it. No network, packages or service credentials are needed. Rational results are strings; the few square-root approximations are labeled. JSON null means unavailable, not zero. The public run(data) validates a full case, derives the witness moments, ranks every grid pair, and returns cash, stress, risk and implementation records without printing or mutating input. Rejection counts overlap because one candidate may violate several rules.

Change γ, a forecast witness, or a limit separately and explain the economic intervention. Maintain the fixed units, date order and mandate conventions. The benchmark must remain feasible under its own costs and limits; contradictory edits are rejected. The model is intentionally bounded to two funded mandates and these dates. If an edit makes the partial-fill buy illustration inapplicable, the output labels it unavailable. The checker independently reconstructs the full feasible ranking, funding boundaries, examples and exercise interventions, then runs the distributed bundle in isolated normal and optimized Python modes. Reproducibility supports the audit trail; it does not certify that synthetic inputs are real forecasts.

8. Exercises and complete solutions

Use exact fractions or enough decimals to preserve the constraints. Each exercise is worth 10 points under its stated rubric. These are chapter practice criteria; the separate Volume 9 examination and integrated project remain distinct requirements.

  1. Moment and risk proof. From the independent Z and U construction, derive both means and all three distinct covariance entries. Prove positive definiteness. For 370/430, derive the variance contributions and active variance without reading the output. Explain why grants appear in expected reserve but not in this planning variance.
  2. Budget and benchmark repair. An analyst proposes benchmark holdings 400 equity, 400 bonds and 200 cash, while separately reporting an entry fee of 1. Reconstruct the correct budget, its planning reserve, variance and inflation/funding reserve. Quantify the overstatement from the analyst's error. Decide whether inherited 300/400 is compliant with the new active-risk limit.
  3. Decision versus preference. Verify J for the winner and the 370/420 runner-up. Find the γ at which those two tie, holding inputs and constraints fixed. State whether that two-portfolio crossing proves a global switch. Then use the full finite set to report the global choices at γ = 2 and γ = 6, with their scores.
  4. Liquidity boundaries. Keep selected positions and the 20 cash buffer. Derive the largest date-1 grant payable without the line and with the full line. For a grant of 200, find the smallest draw preserving the buffer. Under equity −15%, bonds −12% and a date-2 grant of 60, calculate the resulting terminal reserve and any floor shortfall. Distinguish paying a bill from passing both-date policy.
  5. Repair and optimal borrowing. Reconstruct the outside-design case with grants 240/60 and returns −25%/−8%. Show the payment and buffer gaps at maximum draw. Calculate the minimum date-1 contribution that passes both dates at draws zero and 25; prove which minimizes outside funding over all permitted draws. Explain why a contribution is not an investment return.
  6. Execution transfer. Suppose two equity lots, rather than one, are unfilled; bonds still reach 430. Under the +12%/+1% reporting case and grants 150/50, find actual holdings, fee, cash, total and active variance, terminal reserve, implementation gap relative to intended 370/430, and total gap relative to the frozen benchmark. Specify the required governance response.
  7. Input challenge and constraint proof. (a) Set the active-variance limit to zero without changing anything else. Prove which risky holdings are feasible and calculate the corresponding score. (b) Restore the limit 36 and subtract 0.02 from every equity witness return. Show why covariance is unchanged, compute the selected portfolio's revised mean and score, and identify the global winner. Why do the two interventions answer different questions?
  8. Committee decision and evidence critique. Write a short committee decision using the filled IPS and report. Address this claim: “The exact optimum passes all stresses, extra cash lowers risk, and the annual reserve was above 650, so we should certify the manager's skill and remove review requirements.” Give a defensible authorization, two material limits, a breach response, an evidence request and a next-review rule. State what the model cannot establish.
Solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Coherent moments and two risk measures

    E[Z] = E[U] = 0 gives means 0.10 and 0.06. Var(Z) = 1; E[U²] = 2(7/26)(13/100)² = 91/10000. Independence removes cross terms. Hence equity variance is 1/25 = 0.04, bond variance is 9/10000+91/10000 = 1/100, and covariance is (1/5)(3/100) = 3/500 = 0.006. For any nonzero (s,t), variance of 0.20sZ+0.03tZ+tU is (0.20s+0.03t)²+0.0091t², strictly positive. This also proves positive definiteness without relying only on the determinant.

    For 370/430, Σh = (17.38,6.52), and the contribution numerators are 370×17.38 = 6430.6 and 430×6.52 = 2803.6; total 9234.2. Active positions are −30/+30, giving 0.04(900)+0.012(−900)+0.01(900) = 34.2. Planning grants and cash costs are deterministic; their constants affect the mean but vanish when subtracting the expected reserve. Random correlated grants would require a different variance expression. Rubric: means/covariance 4; positive-definite proof 2; total/active risk 3; grant qualification 1.

  2. One currency unit cannot be invested twice

    The benchmark trades 100 equity and no bonds, so K = 1 and c = 199. The corrected planning reserve is 440+424+202.9999−151.5−50 = 865.4999. Variance is 6400+1920+1600 = 9920. The inflation/funding reserve is 340+352+202.9999−181.8−60 = 653.1999. Retaining cash 200 would allocate 1001 in positions plus fee and inflate either terminal reserve by 1.0201. It would also exaggerate date-1 cash by 1.01.

    Inherited 300/400 needs no trade cost, but its active holdings are (−100,0) and active variance is 400 > 36. Its total variance 3600+1440+1600 = 6640 being below the benchmark's variance does not establish active compliance. Rubric: entry budget 2; planning/stress reserves 3; variance/error size 3; inherited breach explanation 2.

  3. Local comparisons are not a full decision certificate

    The winner's score is 864.452915−0.002(9234.2) = 845.984515. The runner-up has fee 0.8, cash 209.2 and score 864.104920−0.002(9104.8) = 845.895320. Their score difference for general γ is 0.347995−γ(129.4)/2000. It vanishes at 69,599/12,940 ≈ 5.378593509. At smaller γ the first of these two wins; at larger γ the second wins.

    This is only their crossing. Another of the 28 feasible points can dominate both, so it does not prove the global optimizer switches between them. Full enumeration at γ = 2 gives 400/400, with score 865.4999−9.92 = 855.5799. At γ = 6 it gives 370/400, with score 863.408930−26.556 = 836.852930. The feasible set is unchanged because γ occurs only in the objective. Rubric: two scores 2; exact crossing 3; global-switch caveat 2; both full-set results 3.

  4. A loan can cure one constraint while leaving another broken

    Cash before the bill is 1.01(199.15) = 201.1415. Preserving 20 without borrowing permits a maximum bill 181.1415; drawing the full 25 raises this to 206.1415. A bill of 200 needs D = 200+20−201.1415 = 18.8585, within the line. Then cash after payment is exactly 20.

    The mandates distribute 314.5+378.4 = 692.9. Cash becomes 20.2; loan repayment is 1.08(18.8585) = 20.36718. After grant 60, reserve is 692.9+20.2−20.36718−60 = 632.73282, short of 650 by 17.26718. The bill and buffer are funded, but the reserve-floor test fails. A new committed contribution or changed authorized grants would need an additional dated calculation. Rubric: boundaries 3; draw and repayment 3; final reserve/gap 3; distinction 1.

  5. Close the outside funds as well as the investment ledger

    At D = 25, available cash 226.1415 is 13.8585 short of the bill 240 and 33.8585 short of bill plus buffer. Adding only 33.8585 leaves final reserve 606.3. The two-date contribution is X(25) = 33.8585+43.7/1.01 = 15,579,417/202,000. At zero borrowing, interim cash alone needs 58.8585, but the terminal bound requires 15,229,417/202,000. That contribution leaves cash 3690/101 after the first bill and reserve exactly 650 after the second.

    The terminal bound at zero exceeds the cash bound; as D rises it increases at 7/101 per unit while the cash bound falls at one per unit. It thus remains the binding positive bound throughout [0,25]. Its minimum is at D = 0. The contribution difference is 175/101. A donor paying X loses X cash when the fund receives it; describing the fund's increase as investment performance omits that external outlay. An actual matched-funding comparison must preserve the contribution date and amount. Rubric: two gaps/partial repair 3; both full repairs 3; minimizing proof 3; contribution interpretation 1.

  6. Preserve every unfilled lot in the comparison

    Actual positions are 350/430. Entry fee is 0.50+0.15 = 0.65; cash is 219.35. Total variance is 4900+1806+1849 = 8555. Active positions (−50,+30) give 100−18+9 = 91, an even larger breach than the one-lot case despite lower total risk.

    At date 1, cash becomes 221.5435 and then 71.5435 after the grant. At date 2 cash is 72.258935; equity pays 392 and bonds 434.3. Final reserve is 392+434.3+72.258935−50 = 848.558935. Relative to intended reserve 850.352915, the implementation gap is −1.79398, twice the one-lot effect because the two missed buys and saved fees scale linearly in this region of the fee rule. Relative to benchmark 853.4999, the total gap is −4.940965. The policy-selection gap remains −3.146985, and the two pieces sum correctly.

    The officer must disclose the unfilled amount and breach, preserve the benchmark and seek the stipulated exception/remedy before the window closes; a hypothetical later fill cannot be assumed. The independent reviewer verifies the record and the committee owns the exception decision. Rubric: holdings/cost/cash 2; both risks 2; dated reserve 2; attribution 2; response 2.

  7. Change authority and information separately

    (a) Since Σ is positive definite, aᵀΣa = 0 if and only if a = 0. A zero active-variance ceiling therefore forces x = y = 400. Its own fee/cash and other constraints pass, so there is exactly one feasible pair, with score 845.6599. The cash position must be 199, not 200; zero active variance alone would not detect a deterministic cash-budget error.

    (b) Subtracting 0.02 from every equity return also subtracts 0.02 from its mean. Each centered equity return is unchanged, preserving its variance and covariance with bonds. At 370/430 the expected reserve falls by 370(0.02) = 7.4 to 857.052915; score falls to 838.584515. The hard constraints and design stresses are unchanged. Comparing all 28 feasible records with their revised means confirms 370/430 remains the global winner. This is a forecast intervention, whereas part (a) changes authorized active risk. One must not label tighter authority as stronger evidence or a revised mean as permission to break limits. Rubric: SPD uniqueness and score 4; centered-return proof 2; revised numbers/global check 3; distinction 1.

  8. An accountable decision has conditions

    Illustrative decision. “Authorize 370 equity and 430 bonds under the stated entry-cost contract, retaining 199.15 cash, subject to verification of actual fills and the dated grants. Keep 400/400 with cash 199 as the frozen strategic comparison. The target meets the disclosed covariance, cash and two design-stress limits and is the exact score winner on our authorized grid. Its advantage is small and conditional on synthetic forecasts and our selected risk preference.”

    “The outside-design event is unfunded without new committed resources; a zero-line contribution of approximately 75.393153465 is one full repair under its stated conditions, not an available asset today. Lower total risk does not imply lower active risk: the partial fill has active variance 58.6. Record and escalate that breach; do not change the benchmark. Request traceable return and grant estimates, valuation/fee evidence and forecast sensitivity before treating the numerical inputs as operational. Review obligations monthly and before grant payments, and authorize a fresh allocation after date-2 maturity.”

    The quoted claim fails in four ways: “all stresses” means only two selected scenarios; a covariance score does not exhaust risk; good ending wealth cannot authorize a past breach; and one outcome cannot identify skill. The model cannot certify performance persistence, real-market probabilities, perpetual solvency, legal suitability or independent governance quality. Other portfolio choices can earn full credit if supported by an explicitly changed, authorized objective and a complete feasible ledger. Rubric: concrete authorized action/benchmark 2; two material limits 2; breach response/ownership 2; evidence request 2; review rule and honest inference 2. An unfunded negative cash path or retrospective benchmark substitution requires remediation even if the prose is persuasive.

9. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back prompt. In three minutes, explain why a feasible portfolio, an attractive modeled score and good realized performance are different claims. Use Larch to show why cash, borrowing and authority must appear in the same investment decision.

Answer benchmark. Feasibility means satisfying the stated grid, costs and constraints at their actual dates; 370/430 passes while the inherited portfolio fails active risk. The score ranks feasible choices under supplied moments and γ, so changing preferences can select the benchmark even with unchanged opportunities. Realized performance compares outcomes with preserved dates, costs and benchmark; one partial fill can lower total risk yet breach active risk. Borrowing funds a date-1 payment only by creating a date-2 repayment, while a new contribution is outside cash rather than a return. The IPS assigns who may approve changes and requires an honest exception record. Full credit requires the distinction between a proof, a policy preference and evidence about the world.

Delayed check 1. Without opening the lab, suppose date-1 grant becomes 181.1415 and no borrowing is used. What cash remains, and does this prove terminal feasibility? Answer: exactly 20 remains. Terminal feasibility still needs the asset returns and date-2 bill; the cash boundary proves only the interim condition.

Delayed check 2. A report shows active variance zero. Does that certify the budget or acceptable total risk? Answer: no. With SPD it identifies risky positions equal to the benchmark under this covariance model, but a deterministic missing fee can still misstate cash, and the benchmark's total risk and obligations need their own tests. Here the budget-correct comparator has variance 9920 and cash 199.

Delayed check 3. The selected inflation reserve is 654.252915 and the board raises its required floor to 660 without changing assets. Can the manager simply retain the old optimum? Answer: it fails the revised floor by 5.747085; the benchmark also fails by 6.8001. The input contract rejects an infeasible declared benchmark. Reconsider allocation, grants, funding and the comparison through authorized policy revision; do not present the old 28-pair certificate as valid under new constraints.

Delayed check 4. Why is a line draw of 25 plus an external contribution of 33.8585 insufficient in the reverse stress? Answer: it restores interim cash to 20 but, after mandate proceeds, grant 60 and repayment 27, leaves reserve 606.3. There remains a 43.7 terminal shortfall. The full date-1 contribution at that draw must be 77.125826733, approximately.

10. Sources and next work

The 2010 CFA Institute IPS paper was inspected for its scope, governance, objectives, liquidity, policy-portfolio and monitoring discussions. It provides institutional context, not Larch's numbers or legal authority. The previously inspected MIT portfolio lectures support mean-variance terminology, Sharpe's article supports the ex-ante comparison, and the dated GIPS methodological discussion supports preserving flow and fee perimeters. All case names, policies, moments, proofs, ledgers and problems here are original.

This chapter closes the investments sequence by making valuation, risk, evidence and implementation answer to an investor's purpose. The separate Volume 9 assessment and substantial project remain a distinct production and learner-assessment requirement. Planned Volume 10 develops fixed-income and derivative tools; additional instruments must be added with their full cash, collateral and risk contracts. A larger menu does not remove the need for a feasible mandate or accountable decisions.

Sources and further study

  • CFA Institute — Elements of an Investment Policy Statement for Institutional Investors (May 2010) — Dated methodological reference for relating a customized institutional mandate to objectives, responsibilities, liquidity, a policy benchmark, risk monitoring, reporting and rebalancing. The Larch policy, all limits and every numerical example are original author choices, not source recommendations or compliance claims.
  • CFA Institute — GIPS Standards Handbook for Firms, Explanation of Provisions in Sections1–8 (November2020), scoped calculation discussion — Flow-boundary time-weighted linking, money-weighted interpretation, Modified Dietz approximation limitations and explicit fee perimeters. This dated methodological reference does not certify library or learner compliance.
  • Andrew W. Lo, MIT 15.401 Finance Theory I — Lectures 13–14: Risk Analytics and Portfolio Theory (2007–2008) — Scoped teaching reference for the mean-variance criterion, efficient upper frontier, safe-asset combinations and excess-return-to-volatility interpretation. Original chapter separately proves SPD solutions and their sign, normalization and constraint boundaries.
  • William F. Sharpe — The Arithmetic of Active Management (1991) — Value-weighted aggregate active/passive arithmetic and the need for an identified feasible benchmark; higher net active costs are an explicit condition, not a universal empirical claim.
